parts.text: The ticket's premise that this is computable from data tetel already holds survives contact with the code for every input this design needs
and the shape of that data decides most of the design.
Prose and claim logs both ship inside the snapshot beside the memo
every event in them is timestamped
and the citation edge a paragraph carries is a field on the prose event itself.
Two details the ticket does not mention narrow what can be built.
Neither `prose::load_all` nor `claims::load_all` surfaces a timestamp
both replay their log into a struct that keeps only a revision count
so this check reads the JSONL directly rather than reusing the loaded types the rest of `check` works from.
And a prose block's id exists only inside the workspace:
`compose::render` writes the block's text and its `*cites:` marker and nothing else
so a residue line that says `P4` names something a reader holding only the memo cannot find.
Claim ids do not have that problem
the rendered ledger prints the workspace id verbatim.

parts.text: The ticket's phrase "the last grounding pass" is not merely ambiguous
as its own open questions suspected
read literally it is self-defeating
and this is the design's first and largest departure.
Every grounding pass is briefed on every claim in the ledger
whether or not it has been graded before
so a pass that finds nothing to change still appends a fresh record against the unchanged wording.
The two memos already in this tree show what that produces
one claim carrying ten records on a single unchanged digest
written by three passes across nearly half an hour
and another graded `qualifies` twice by different passes a quarter of an hour apart on text nobody touched.
Anchor the comparison at the most recent grading and the anchor walks forward every round
fix-round prose written in round three stops being "since the last pass" the moment round four runs
even though no pass has ever read a word of the prose.
On the ticket's own account of it
the trail this residue is named after ran six rounds.
So the anchor is the earliest record grading a claim's current wording
the moment that wording first entered proof.
A later pass over unchanged text cannot move it
and only a revision of the claim itself
followed by a grading of the new wording

With the anchor fixed
the rule almost states itself
and the places where it does not are the places attack put there.
A prose block is listed when it is a paragraph rather than a heading
it cites at least one id
at least one cited id resolves to a ledger claim that is in proof
and the block's text timestamp is later than the latest first proof among those in-proof citations.
"In proof" is not a new predicate
it is the digest comparison `analyze_ledger` already performs
empty-digest grandfathering included.
The block's text timestamp is the earliest event in its history whose text and citation list both equal the current ones.
Neither half of that definition was in the first draft of this design and neither is decoration
the next two sections are about what each one closes.
The two quantifier choices the ticket left open fall out of the anchor rather than being decided by taste.
take the earliest in-proof record
because that is when the wording settled.
take the latest of those
because a block is not anchored until its evidence base has settled
taking the earliest instead would list every paragraph whose text merely postdates its first-graded citation
which is nearly all of them.
Both memos already in this tree list nothing
and that includes the two real post-pass prose revisions they contain between them
tet29's P4 and tet28's P18.
Each was rewritten in a fix round after a pass had run
and each is correctly silent for the same reason
each also cites a claim revised in that same round
whose new wording entered proof only afterwards.
The maximum is doing exactly the work it was chosen for.
That also means the listing behaviour had to be tested on constructions appended to those logs rather than on a real defect
move a tet29 paragraph past its claim's first proof and touch no claim
and it is listed alone.
NONE
On the ticket's first open question
creation or revision
the residue is about neither act specifically but about the text's age
the timestamp is derived from the block's events without caring whether the earliest one bearing its current wording was a creation or a rewrite.
The exposure is the same in both directions
since a paragraph written fresh under already-graded claims rests on them exactly as ungradedly as a rewritten one
and the ticket's own vector could have arrived either way.
Counting creations also cannot inflate the list through paragraphs added to carry a new assertion under a new claim
and the reason is mechanical rather than statistical
a claim not yet in proof cannot anchor a block at all
and once a pass has put it in proof that first proof necessarily postdates a paragraph written before the pass ran.
How often a fix-round paragraph takes that shape rather than resting on old claims is a question about how authors behave
and nothing here measures it.
What creation-counting does catch is the case worth catching
a new paragraph written under nothing but old
settled claims.

parts.text: What clears a listing is the whole design
and it took two refutations to get right.
Start with what is easy
a further grounding pass over unchanged wording appends records but cannot move the earliest one
so no amount of re-grounding clears a block
which is correct
since a grounding pass never reads the prose and could not vouch for it if it did.
The first refutation was that reverting a paragraph could not clear it either.
Prose history is append-only
so a revert appends a later timestamp
keyed on the last event
restoring the settled wording would have left the listing standing forever.
Looking the timestamp up by content rather than by event order fixes that.
The second refutation is sharper and came from attacking the fix.
Keyed on text alone
an author could leave the text untouched and revise only the citations
an act `prose::revise` does not even inspect
and one the `cite` parameter was added to permit
pointing the paragraph at some claim the fix round had legitimately revised and regraded.
The anchor moved forward
the timestamp stayed frozen
the line went out
and the machine partition stayed green.
A residue that can be silenced by an act indistinguishable from good authoring is worse than no residue
because it certifies.
Keying the timestamp on the text and the citation list together closes it
change either and the timestamp moves with it.
A third construction closed with it
an old uncited paragraph handed a citation to an already-settled claim
which under the earlier rule entered the list with a timestamp predating everything and was permanently unlistable.
So two things clear a listing
restoring the text and citations the claims settled under
and revising or adding a cited claim and having the new wording graded.
The second is precisely what the finding asks for
because the defect being surfaced is prose asserting something no claim carries.
The cost is that neither is cheap
and it is worth being blunt about how large it can get.
Nothing in the rule bounds the number of blocks it can reach
an author who flow-edits every paragraph of a settled memo will see every paragraph listed
and on a memo shaped like tet29
twelve blocks
every one a cited paragraph
no headings among them
that is all twelve.
So what separates this from the `no scope declared` line that once printed once per claim is not that a full sweep is impossible.
It is that a full sweep here would report something the author did
not something tetel is
that it is about this document rather than about the tool
and that two concrete acts clear it.
NONE
Of everything the ticket left open
the doubt about comparing timestamps across workspaces is the one that deserved its suspicion
and it does not dissolve.
The claim to be careful with is what exactly is new here.
Ordering timestamps written by different processes is not
the mint-window check already places refusals against a mint
and each of those lines was appended by a separate invocation.
What is new is that the two sides come from different *workspaces*
one authoring
one grounding
where every existing comparison has stayed inside one
and where every check that could have compared a claim against its evidence used a digest instead.
The comparison is sound in unit
both timestamps come from a `now_unix` whose body is token-for-token the same in the only two places the worktree defines it
so the same epoch and the same unit with no timezone term between them.
What nothing in either record establishes is that the two processes read the same wall clock.
The bound that follows is exact
and the design's position is that it must be printed rather than left implicit

a reported ordering can be wrong only if the grounding process's clock differed from the authoring workspace's by more than the interval between the prose edit and the pass that first put the cited claims in proof.
Choosing first proof over last pass is what makes that interval a grounding round rather than seconds in the case this residue exists for
but nothing measured here bounds it from below
and no claim is made that it is always large.

parts.text: So the question becomes whether the digest-shaped alternative the ticket hoped for exists.
Two were examined
and no claim is made that a third could not be found.
The sharp one
a record carrying a digest of the prose it vouches for
the exact analogue of `out_of_proof`
cannot be built
for a structural reason rather than an oversight.
`out_of_proof` compares digests because a record carries a digest of the very text it graded.
No record names or digests a prose block anywhere in its shape
and the brief a pass receives is id
proposition and pin.
Putting a prose digest into a record would mean the grounding pass reading the prose it exists to grade blind
which trades the independence the whole loop is built on for a residue line.
The weaker one is genuinely constructible and was worked through rather than waved away:
`render --out` could append a publication record
each prose block's text digest
each claim's proposition digest and whether anything grades it
and the residue would then be an ordinal comparison between successive publications with no clock in it at all.
It is rejected on resolution
and the reason is structural too.
A log that samples only when the author renders cannot order two events that fall inside one interval
and a grading followed by a prose edit followed by a single render is one interval.
On the ticket's own account
that is the shape the finding took.
The clock-free formulation would have been silent on it.
That is the trade
stated plainly
the timestamp comparison buys the one ordering an interval-sampled log cannot
and pays for it with a bound it prints.
NONE
The vacuous case needs no special handling
because the in-proof test already does the work
but which test turned out to matter
and attack decided it rather than argument.
A memo with no evidence ledger
and a memo halfway through its first draft
no cited claim is in proof
so there is no first proof to compare against.
The design first required *every* cited claim to be in proof
on the tidy-looking ground that a paragraph resting on an ungrounded claim is already in front of the reader under a line about that claim.
It is not the same reader service
C99` is a line about a claim
not about the paragraph
it made adding a record-less citation a way to silence any listing at all
with a clean machine partition
since a claim with no records is human-owed rather than out of proof.
So the test is existential
one in-proof citation is enough to anchor a block
and a record-less citation contributes nothing to the anchor and cannot suppress anything.
Non-overlap survives for what is still skipped
a block every one of whose citations is ungrounded or out of proof is already reported
under `ungrounded` or under a machine failure.
Two populations remain outside the rule entirely.
which cite nothing by construction
and paragraphs that cite nothing by choice.
The second is a real gap
an uncited paragraph is the one place a false assertion can sit with no citation edge to compare it against
and that belongs in the printed non-coverage list rather than in a footnote here.

One property is worth settling explicitly
because it is where a rule of this family usually goes wrong
the trigger interprets no English.
It is not keyed on deciding from a memo's prose that the memo is in scope.
The citation edge is a field the author set with `--cites`
the heading flag is a boolean on the same event
and the ordering is a comparison of integers taken off two logs.
Text is consumed in exactly two places
and both are byte comparisons.
The in-proof test feeds a claim's proposition into sha256
and finding a block's text timestamp means testing each of its past versions for equality with the current text and citation list
which reads every version of every paragraph as bytes.
Nothing anywhere parses a sentence
matches a phrase
or forms a view about what a paragraph is about.
What stays undecidable is the verdict rather than the trigger
whether a listed paragraph really does assert something its claims do not carry.
That is not narrowed
hinted at or scored here.
It goes whole to the reader
which is what the human-owed partition is
the one whose own opening sentence ends "none of this is settled by a passing check".

parts.text: Every input this design needs is present in data tetel already ships
so the mechanism is buildable
but the ticket's anchor is wrong in a way that would have made it silent on the very finding it cites.
"Since the last grounding pass" walks forward every round
because every pass is briefed on every claim and re-grades unchanged wording
so fix-round prose stops being recent as soon as another round runs.
The anchor is therefore the earliest record grading a claim's current wording
the moment that wording first entered proof
and a block is listed when its text postdates the latest such moment among the claims it cites that are in proof.
That single change settles the ticket's other ambiguities as side effects
it decides earliest-versus-latest in both quantifiers
it empties the vacuous cases without a special rule
it makes creation and revision the same question
and it stops a grounding pass from blessing prose it never read.
Two smaller corrections were forced by attack rather than reached by design
and both are on the other side of the comparison.
A block's timestamp is looked up by its text *and* its citation list together
not by its last event
keyed on the event
restoring a paragraph's settled wording could never clear the line
and keyed on text alone
a citation-only revision could silence one in seconds using a claim the fix round had legitimately produced.
And the in-proof test is existential
because requiring every citation to be in proof let a single record-less citation suppress a block with nothing red to show for it.
What none of this removes is a cross-process clock comparison
which neither digest-shaped alternative examined here can replace
because no evidence record has anywhere to put a digest of prose and the pass that would compute one is required not to read it.
That bound is printed once
in a preamble above the entries it qualifies.

parts.text: The clause that is wrong is the one the ticket did not think it was making.
The ticket's first constraint
an explicitly named path must still be read
only traversal skips
"the rule `git` and `rg` apply to ignored files"
is stated as though grep already obeyed it.
A file named explicitly on grep's command line is skipped when `--exclude` matches it
and a directory named explicitly as the recursion root is skipped when `--exclude-dir` matches it
in both cases the identical command without the flag finds the match
so the flag is what removed it.
Exactly one of the three arrangements behaves the way the constraint describes
and it is the one nobody would have doubted:
`--exclude-dir` does not suppress a file that is named explicitly and searched non-recursively from inside an excluded directory.
So the explicit-path exception is not something this design can obtain by choosing flags.
It has to be implemented in tetel
by deciding when to pass the flags at all.
NONE
The rendered-memo test has a second problem
and it is in the ticket's one-line implementation sketch rather than in its principle.
The sketch says
glob for `*.tetel` directories under the search root
strip the suffix
pass the result as `--exclude`.
Both halves of that fail.
A `--exclude` pattern is matched against the name grep constructs for the file from the root it was given
so with a relative root an absolute-path pattern excludes nothing whatsoever and the search silently returns everything
while the same file spelled relative to the root is excluded correctly.
And a suffix-stripped bare basename is not a name
it is a glob that matches that basename anywhere in the tree
which in the measurement removed both a real rendered memo and an unrelated file of the same name that has no snapshot beside it and so is not a memo at all.
A wrong exclusion of that second kind is the worst failure available here
because it hides source from a census under the banner of hiding tetel's own output.
The pattern must be emitted path-prefixed
in whatever spelling the root itself was given in.
NONE

parts.text: The disclosure goes in the whole-search record's label
and it costs nothing in schema.
TET-28 already added exactly one record per `look --grep` whose job is to say where a search started rather than what it hit
a `Search` entry when the grep matched
a `NoMatch` entry when it did not
and never both.
That record is the natural and the only correct home for a statement about what the search did not visit
because the exclusion is a property of the search and not of any file it found.
Putting the text there buys two carriers already built

so the exclusion set is on the page for a reader who has only the committed document
and the pin hashes the label
so two searches with different exclusion sets fingerprint differently even when the text they matched is identical.
It should also be printed in what `look` returns
for the author reading it in the moment
but the printed string is the convenience and the label is the record
which is the opposite of the two shapes this project has already been burned by
a warning with no lifecycle
and a refusal trail missing the refusal that mattered.

and no others.

parts.text: The sketch left the event's home open between `prose.jsonl` and a sibling log.
The evidence closes it
and not on grounds of taste.
`ProseEvent` is an internally-tagged enum over two variants
and the workspace's line reader turns any single unparseable line into an error over the entire log.
A third variant is therefore not a compatible addition:
I wrote a scratch workspace whose prose log held one ordinary `Create` followed by one `Ack`
and the build at this pin refused the whole file
including the `Create` it understood perfectly well.
Every older build encountering such a snapshot would lose its ability to read prose at all
which is a far worse outcome than the residue line this design exists to clear.
The field-level `#[serde(default)]` precedent already in both variants does not extend to a new variant.
NONE
So the event lives in its own append-only log
and the snapshot manifest gains a tenth entry.
Three properties
make the failure direction one-way
and the third is the one I had to be shown twice.
The manifest is the first
it is an explicit enumeration precisely so that shipping a new workspace file is a decision rather than an accident
so a build predating the entry never opens the file and prints exactly the listing TET-30 shipped.
The second is that the ack log only grows
which holds cheaply here because the file does not exist yet
nothing in the tool today can remove or truncate a file it has never heard of
its only writer will be an appending verb
and no withdrawal verb ships.
That was where an earlier draft of this section stopped
and stopping there was wrong.
Monotonicity is a property of one workspace's log
the mechanism runs over a snapshot.
Nothing binds a memo to the workspace that rendered it
the flag is free on every invocation
and the writer skips a file the current workspace lacks rather than removing it.
So render a memo once from a workspace holding an acknowledgement
then again from a workspace that never held one
a rebuilt state directory
a second machine
and the old ack log survives beside the new prose and claims.
That is a superset
and it suppresses a block the true state would list
The third property closes it
the ack records the identity of the workspace that minted it
and suppression requires that identity to match the one the snapshot ships.
A log from elsewhere is then void rather than honoured
and the failure returns to over-reporting.
NONE
Now the problem that buys all of that.
TET-30 names two acts that clear a listing
and for the case this design is about
an edit that corrects the prose and touches no claim's proposition
neither describes what the author did.
Restoring the text puts the typo back.
The other act splits.
Revising a cited claim so its new wording can be graded means changing a claim that is correct
and it is worse than merely expensive
out-of-proof is a machine-check disjunct and this residue is not
so that route turns a green run red and keeps it red until another grounding pass lands
in order to silence a line that by construction never failed anything.
Adding a citation to a freshly minted claim is cheaper
an ungrounded claim is human-owed
so nothing reddens
but it still means inventing a claim the paragraph never needed and buying a pass to grade it.
An author who reads their paragraph against its claims
finds it faithful
and has nothing to change is left with no honest act at all.
That is the defect
not the listing on first appearance
which is informative
but its permanence after the human act it asks for has been performed.
NONE
The brief called deletion and annotation both doctrine-compatible
and they are not equally good.
Deletion loses a distinction the crate elsewhere insists on keeping
a report from which an acknowledged block has vanished cannot be told from a report on a memo where no post-proof revision ever happened
and this is a tool whose no-rows path exists precisely to say that two states which happen to both be quiet are not the same state.
The cost of printing is also already paid
the entry format carries an author's own reason verbatim today
under `revised because:`
with the source comment insisting it is never paraphrased and calling it the most actionable line the entry has.
NONE
So an acknowledged block moves rather than disappears.
It leaves the group under the "prose revised after the claims it cites settled" preamble
which is what makes the acknowledgement feel like a discharge and not a footnote
and reappears under a single collapsed bullet listing
its line in the document
when it was acknowledged
and the author's own words for why.
Because the reason and the timestamp are recorded but not keyed
more than one ack can match a block at once
and the entry prints the earliest of them
that mirrors the trigger's own use of the earliest event bearing the current wording
and it shows a reader the moment the discharge was first made rather than the latest restatement of it.
The collapse itself is the crate's habit
the residue's preamble is one document-level bullet
adopted on the stated ground that a constant repeated per row buries what is specific to this document.
Leaving the entry in place with an annotation stapled to it would keep the demand standing after it had been met
which is exactly the condition that teaches readers to skim the partition.
NONE
The event records the block
the block's current text and citation list
a digest of each cited claim's proposition as it stands at that moment
the identity of the workspace minting it
and the author's verbatim reason
it carries a timestamp because every workspace event does.
A listing is suppressed exactly when some ack for that block matches all of that
byte for byte
against values the check recomputes
the digests included
and the identity against the one the snapshot itself ships.
One detail here is easy to get wrong and I got it wrong first
the digests are taken over the claim as `claims.jsonl` holds it
not over the ledger-derived proposition the in-proof test must use.
Those two strings differ
rendering replaces embedded newlines with spaces and importing trims the cell
so keying the ack on the trigger's digest would make any claim with an embedded newline or edge whitespace permanently unackable
Both sides of the ack's comparison read the same source
and the snapshot already ships it.
No timestamp is compared anywhere in the predicate.
NONE
The sketch also wanted the ack's timestamp compared against the recomputed anchor.
Working through when that comparison could ever decide anything showed it cannot.
The rule is only ever consulted for a block the trigger has already listed
and listing is precisely the statement that the block timestamp exceeds the anchor
the ack is appended afterwards
to an append-only log
by the same workspace and the same clock function that stamped the prose event.
Barring a clock set backwards mid-session
the ack timestamp is above the block timestamp which is above the anchor
so the clause is true every time it is asked.
Removing it is not a simplification for its own sake
it leaves the suppression predicate with no timestamp comparison anywhere in it
and so the acknowledgement
alone among the moving parts here
does not inherit the two-clock bound that the trigger's own preamble has to print.
NONE
Three properties are worth stating as invariants with tests
and each has a specific mutation that should turn its test red.
Any later edit to the block's text or citations voids the ack
since both are in the key
weaken the comparison to text alone and a citation-only revision
which TET-30 deliberately made list rather than clear
would slip through an old acknowledgement.
Any change to a cited claim's proposition voids the ack
since the key carries that claim's digest
drop the digests and an acknowledgement survives a rewrite of the very claim the paragraph was read against.
And for a memo whose snapshot carries no acknowledgement log
the residue reports exactly what it reports today
because the line reader treats a missing file as an empty log
make that an error instead and every memo rendered before this design would stop checking.
That third invariant is deliberately stated over the residue's findings rather than the report's bytes
because this same design adds lines to the non-coverage list
which prints unconditionally and so changes the bytes of every report the tool will ever write.
It is also about the snapshot and not the workspace
which is worth saying explicitly rather than leaving to be inferred
the check never sees a workspace.
NONE
Underneath those is the property that makes the rest cheap to reason about
the acknowledgement is a filter applied to the trigger's output
never an input to it.
The set of blocks a reader is asked to act on can only shrink
so the design cannot invent a demand.
A stale ack and an unmatched ack both simply fail to suppress
which is indistinguishable from no ack at all.
A corrupt one is the case I first waved through and should not have.
The line reader turns any bad line into an error over the entire log
and the one place this crate swallows that silently
the prose log at check time
defends the silence with a premise that does not transfer
that a corrupt prose log has already reddened provenance before the check gets there.
Keeping acks out of `render` is precisely what makes that false for this file.
So an unreadable acknowledgement log has to redden
joining the existing rule that drift and an unreadable snapshot are machine failures because both are objective contradictions decidable without a human.
That is the single point where this design touches the machine partition
and it touches it for corruption of the record rather than for anything an acknowledgement means.
It is also worth being clear what the digests do not buy
keying on them does not close TET-30's conceded blind spot for prose that ships alongside a claim revision.
It only stops an acknowledgement outliving the state it attested to.
NONE
There is exactly one verb
`prose --ack <id> --why <text>`
on both front ends
as the section on withdrawal explains
deliberately no second one.
It is added to the shared request shape the CLI and the MCP server already funnel through
and here I have to correct something an earlier draft of this memo asserted
that shape is necessary for the two front ends to agree
and it is not sufficient.
This verb is the case that proves it
both times about text.
An acknowledgement carries none
but the MCP parameter struct declares text as a plain required string while the CLI declares it optional
so an ack over MCP is refused by deserialisation before any of the tool's own refusals are reached
and the same ack over the CLI sails through.
Relaxing that field is part of this design.
But relaxing it is not enough
because an absent `--text` on the CLI does not mean absent
both text-consuming arms resolve it through a helper whose empty case reads standard input.
an acknowledgement with no text would sit there blocking on stdin.
So `--text` has to be refused outright in this mode
and the ack arm placed where it can never reach that fallback.
NONE
There is a second thing each front end does that this verb must not inherit.
Mode is selected by an if/else-if chain that builds one request variant and silently drops whatever inputs that variant has no field for
so an ack combined with `--text`
`--cites` or `--before` would discard one without a word
the same shape as the defect this crate already had to fix once
when citations were accepted alongside a revision and thrown away.
All six have to be refused
and `--level` is worth dwelling on because I left it out and an attack pass had to put it back.
On the CLI it is its own flag
consumed by the heading arm but selected by `--heading`
over MCP the two are folded into a single field that is selector and value at once.
An enumeration written while looking at the MCP shape cannot see the CLI's seventh flag.
Of the ack's remaining refusals only two already exist
the block must exist
and `--why` must be non-empty
the latter on literally the test that backs the revise verb's insistence that revisions explain themselves.
Three are new
because creation is deliberately ungated
refusing a heading
refusing an uncited block
and refusing a citation that names no claim.
Each earns its place
a listing exists for neither a heading nor an uncited block
and the ack's key is a digest per cited claim
which an unresolvable id cannot supply.
One refusal that might seem obvious is impossible.
The verb cannot decline to acknowledge a block that is not currently listed
because an authoring workspace holds prose
targets and counters and no evidence records whatsoever
grading records live beside the rendered memo
so at mint time there is no anchor to compute.
Nor is it wanted
acknowledging an unlisted block suppresses nothing.
NONE
Because the residue is computed against a snapshot and the snapshot is written by `render --out`
an ack minted after a render is invisible until the next one.
That sequencing is not new and it is not this design's to fix
everything the check sees about a workspace it sees through the snapshot.
What is this design's to decide is whether the acknowledgement changes the memo's bytes
and it must not
the determinism of `render` in the workspace alone is what makes a drift finding mean anything.
Keeping acks out of the rendered output turns the extra render from an annoyance into a useful signal
it rewrites the snapshot in place and leaves the document byte-identical
so the discharge lands in version control as a change to the record with no change to the argument.
That is a true description of what an acknowledgement is.
NONE
Supersession asks nothing of the design.
Matching is existential over keys
so a later ack with a different key simply does not match
and a duplicate ack for the same key cannot change whether a block is suppressed.
Withdrawal is the harder question
and I have been wrong about it in both directions.
I first designed an `Unack` event
on the reasoning that an author who acknowledged too quickly and cannot yet rewrite the paragraph would otherwise have nothing to say.
Then I removed it
on the reasoning that a negative event is uniquely droppable
and that reasoning survives
though it turned out to matter for a different reason than I gave.
Declining the verb is what keeps the ack log monotone
and monotonicity is what makes a stale snapshot copy a prefix rather than an arbitrary earlier state
which is the whole one-directional guarantee of the section above.
An `Unack` would have broken it
a render by a build predating the log leaves it where the last knowing render put it
so a withdrawal appended afterwards vanishes while the acknowledgement it cancelled survives
the one path by which a negative event is lost and a positive one is not.
And the decision stands on a second leg that was always the stronger.
The case an `Unack` protects is not symmetric with the defect this design exists for
an author who now believes the paragraph is faulty can repair the paragraph
which voids the acknowledgement by changing its key.
That is an honest act
and it is the one they should be taking.
TET-30's defect was precisely that a correct paragraph left its author no act at all.
NONE

parts.text: Stated upfront
before the argument that gets there
the discharge is a new workspace event in its own append-only log
keyed on the block's current text
its citation list
a digest of each cited claim
and the identity of the workspace that minted it
suppressing the listing exactly while all of that still matches what the check recomputes.
A tenth file therefore ships in the snapshot and a new event schema exists
falsifying deliberately the sentence TET-30's memo ends its implementation-surface claim with.
The payment is bounded
but by three properties rather than the two an earlier draft claimed
and only two of them come free
a predating build never opens the new file
and the ack log only grows.
The third had to be added
because a memo is not bound to the workspace that rendered it
and without the identity component a snapshot can carry acknowledgements no workspace on the machine ever made.
The cost also has two shapes
Ordinarily an older build over-reports a line a newer one suppresses.
But because a corrupt ack log reddens
one malformed line makes a new build exit 1 where an old build runs clean
a disagreement about the machine partition rather than about a listing.
`check` names the binary behind every report it writes
so either divergence is attributable
what that does not cover is a reader holding a single old report
with nothing in it to suggest an acknowledgement exists.
For them the answer is the log itself
plain JSON lines beside the memo
readable with no tetel at all.

an acknowledgement records that a human said they re-read the paragraph against its claims
and nothing verifies that they did or judges whether the paragraph is faithful

and the sole place a per-citation judgement can live is inside the author's verbatim reason

letting a reader pair the author's words to the citations themselves

a reason and a timestamp
and none of the quantities the rule derives
not the anchor
not any claim's first proof
not the block timestamp
not even whether the block was listed.
The general ledger needs the events as they stand plus a rule that reads them
which is a re-homing and not a rework.

parts.text: One thing remains to be said
and it belongs with the decision to keep acknowledgements out of the rendered bytes.
Drift is decided by re-rendering the snapshot
and `render` reads exactly five of the nine files a snapshot ships
transplants and facts.
The other four are shipped and never re-rendered
so tampering with them is not drift
and one of those four is the identity file
which already decides whether the report calls a claim self-grounded or independently grounded.
An acknowledgement log joins that group rather than founding it.
A hand-edited snapshot ack log is therefore undetectable by drift
and the honest response is a non-coverage line rather than a bespoke mechanism
guarding acks alone would leave the four existing members unguarded while implying they were not.
That is the last of this design's costs
and like the others it is meant to be read rather than absorbed.
NONE
